def parse_version(version: Sequence[str | int]) -> tuple[int, ...]:
    """Split a version string like "0.20.16" into a tuple of ints, e.g. (0, 20, 16)."""
    if isinstance(version, str):
        version = version.split(".")
    return tuple(int(re.sub(r"\D", "", str(v))) for v in version)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
polars-genson turns JSON into Polars columns in two steps:

  1. Infer a schema. genson reads every row and builds one schema that fits them all: which fields exist, what type each has, which objects are records and which are maps.
  2. Normalise the rows. Each row is rewritten to fit that schema: missing fields are filled with null, values are converted to the field's type, maps are encoded, and scalars are promoted where needed. The result decodes to one consistent set of typed columns.

The pages in this section explain the decisions genson makes along the way. Each shows real output from genson for small inputs.

  • Type mapping: which Polars dtype each kind of JSON value becomes.
  • Nulls, missing keys and empty values: what happens to absent, null and empty values, and to null rows.
  • Maps and records: when an object becomes a struct and when a map, and how to choose.
  • Map types: how a map is held in the Avro schema, in Polars as a pl.Map, in JSON text and in Parquet.
  • Mixed types: what happens when one field holds different kinds of value in different rows.
  • Field order: how genson orders fields, and why that matters when combining output from several inputs.
  • How inference works: the algorithm behind all of the above, from reading the rows to deciding which objects are maps.

docs.title: How inference works
docs.text: genson infers a schema in two passes. The first reads the data and builds one JSON Schema that every row fits. The second rewrites that schema: it decides which objects are maps, merges the different shapes a value takes, and puts union types in a fixed order. This page describes both. The pages before it describe the outcome; this one describes the algorithm, for when you need to know why a schema came out as it did, or what a change to the data will do to it.

docs.title: Pass 1: build a schema from the data
One tree per position in the data
docs.text:
genson parses each JSON string with simd-json and records what it sees in a tree with one node per position in the data: the root, each field of an object, the items of an array, the values of a map. A node records each kind of value seen at its position:

Seen at the position Recorded an object its fields, in the order first seen; the keys present in every object an array one node for all of its items a number integer, until a number that is not an integer is seen: then number a string, boolean, null the type

A position that held more than one kind of value gets a schema for each: scalars become a list of types ({"type": ["null", "string"]}), and an object or array alongside others becomes an anyOf. A field is required when every object seen at that position held it.

wrap_root writes each document inside an object of one field ({"<field>": <document>}) before it is parsed.

docs.title: Many strings: one tree each, then merged
docs.text:
With 10 or more strings, each string gets a tree of its own on the thread pool. The trees are then merged, in input order, into one: fields are united in the order first seen, the required keys are those required in every tree, and a number position becomes number if it is number in any tree. Merging two trees gives the same schema as reading all of their data into one tree.

  • Repeated schemas are merged once. Each string's tree is hashed as it is built, and a tree whose schema equals one already merged is skipped. Rows of the same shape are common, so this saves most of the merging. (The processed_count that inference reports is the number of distinct schemas merged.)
  • The merge runs in parallel across fields. When the trees being merged are all objects, each field of the root is merged on its own thread, and so on down the tree while there are enough trees to make it worthwhile. Each field still takes its values in input order, so the result does not depend on the number of threads.
  • max_builders bounds memory. Strings are processed in chunks of max_builders; each chunk's trees are merged before the next chunk is parsed (see Process large inputs).
  • Fields forced to be maps (force_field_types={"field": "map"}) are turned into maps in each string's tree before the merge, so that their values are merged across strings as map values rather than as fields.

With fewer than 10 strings, each string is read into the same tree in turn. Within one string, the documents of NDJSON (and arrays of 10 or more items anywhere) are read on several threads and merged the same way.

docs.title: Pass 2: rewrite the schema
docs.text:
The merged tree is written out as a JSON Schema, and genson walks it from the root, carrying each field's name down so that options naming fields apply. At each object, the first of these rules that applies decides what happens:

  1. A field in force_scalar_promotion holding a scalar becomes a record with one field, <field>__<type> (for example datavalue__string).
  2. A field in force_field_types becomes a map ("map"), whose value schema is the values' common schema, unified as below if they differ, or else string; or stays a record ("record").
  3. An anyOf of scalars and records, with wrap_scalars on (the default), becomes one record: each scalar is promoted to a record of one field <field>__<type>, and the records are unified.
  4. An object that was empty in every row, with map_threshold=0, becomes a map of null (a record with no fields cannot be written to Parquet).
  5. An object holding a field named in force_parent_field_types as "record", or a field in force_scalar_promotion, stays a record.

  6. An object becomes a map when it has at least map_threshold keys, is not the root (unless no_root_map=False), and

    • all of its values are the same record; or else
    • it has at most map_max_required_keys required keys (if that is set), and its values' schemas are the same once nullability is set aside or, with unify_maps, they unify.

    The map's value schema is that common schema.

Then genson goes on into the object's fields, an array's items and a map's values.

docs.title: Unifying value schemas
docs.text:
Unification merges the schemas of a candidate map's values into one, when they are of one kind:

Values Unified as arrays an array of the items unified; an array only ever seen empty fits any array maps (and empty records) a map of the values unified records a record of every field seen: unified field by field, required and non-null where every record requires the field, nullable otherwise scalars of one type that type, nullable

Within a record field, two schemas that differ only in being nullable merge into the nullable one, and with wrap_scalars a scalar that meets a record (or a scalar of another type) is promoted under <field>__<type>. Array items unify the same way, and there a scalar among records is promoted too. Values of different kinds that none of this reconciles (an array and a record, say) do not unify, and the object stays a record. Nor is an object unified when one of its keys is named in no_unify.

docs.title: Union order
docs.text: Finally, every list of types is put in a fixed order: null first, then containers (map, array, object), then scalars from the narrowest (boolean, integer, number, string). A ["null", T] pair keeps its order.

docs.title: Field order
docs.text: genson keeps fields in the order they first appear in the JSON. The order is part of the output: it's the order of the columns and of the fields inside each struct.

docs.title: Within one object: document order
docs.text:
An object's fields keep the order of its keys, however many keys it has:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

keys = ["zeta", "alpha", "mu", "beta"]
row = "{" + ", ".join(f'"{k}": 1' for k in keys) + "}"
print(pl.DataFrame({"j": [row]}).genson.infer_polars_schema("j"))

Schema({'zeta': Int64, 'alpha': Int64, 'mu': Int64, 'beta': Int64})

docs.title: Across rows: first-seen order
docs.text:
When rows have different keys, a field's position is where it was first seen, reading the rows in order:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"b": 1}', '{"a": 1, "b": 2}', '{"c": 3, "a": 4}']})
print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j"))

Schema({'b': Int64, 'a': Int64, 'c': Int64})

b comes first because the first row has it; a appears in the second row and c in the third. The same holds for the fields of merged records, such as the values of a map under unify_maps (see Maps and records).

docs.title: Determinism
docs.text: The same input always gives the same field order, on every run. (Before 0.9.0, objects with more than 32 keys could come out in a different order on each run.)

docs.title: Combining output from several inputs
docs.text: Because the order depends on which rows are seen first, two inputs with the same fields can still produce different field orders: another file may simply list its keys or rows in a different order. When you combine output from several inputs, put their fields into one fixed order first, for example the order of a schema you keep for the dataset, so the combined columns and structs line up.

docs.title: Map types: Avro, Polars and Parquet
docs.text:
Once genson has decided that an object is a map, with keys that are data rather than field names (see Maps and records), that map passes through several formats on its way to a column. This page follows one map through each of them.

Where A map of language to label JSON input {"en": "Hi", "es": "Hola"} The inferred Avro schema {"type": "map", "values": "string"} A Polars column pl.Map(pl.String, pl.String) A typed Parquet file a Parquet MAP, Arrow map<string, string> The kv encoding pl.List(pl.Struct({"key": pl.String, "value": pl.String}))

docs.title: In the schema: an Avro map
docs.text:
genson records its decision in the schema it infers. In Avro, a map is a type of its own, with one type for all its values:

import json
import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": [
    '{"id": 1, "labels": {"en": "Hi", "es": "Hola"}}',
    '{"id": 2, "labels": {"fr": "Bonjour"}}',
]})
schema = df.genson.infer_json_schema("j", map_threshold=1, avro=True)
print(json.dumps(schema["fields"][1], indent=2))

{
  "name": "labels",
  "type": {
    "name": "labels",
    "type": "map",
    "values": "string"
  }
}

Avro map keys are always strings, so every map genson infers has string keys.

docs.title: In Polars: pl.Map
docs.text:
normalise_json and infer_polars_schema give a map as a pl.Map. Each row holds its own keys, and only those:

out = df.genson.normalise_json("j", map_threshold=1)
print(out)

shape: (2, 2)
┌─────┬────────────────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ labels                     │
│ --- ┆ ---                        │
│ i64 ┆ map[str, str]              │
╞═════╪════════════════════════════╡
│ 1   ┆ {"en": "Hi", "es": "Hola"} │
│ 2   ┆ {"fr": "Bonjour"}          │
└─────┴────────────────────────────┘

Polars' map namespace reads it, for example map.get for one key, map.keys for the keys, and map.entries for the key/value pairs:

labels = pl.col("labels")
print(out.select(labels.map.get("en").alias("en"), labels.map.keys().alias("keys")))

shape: (2, 2)
┌──────┬──────────────┐
│ en   ┆ keys         │
│ ---  ┆ ---          │
│ str  ┆ list[str]    │
╞══════╪══════════════╡
│ Hi   ┆ ["en", "es"] │
│ null ┆ ["fr"]       │
└──────┴──────────────┘

docs.title: As JSON text: map_encoding
docs.text:
With decode=False, normalise_json writes each row as a JSON string, and map_encoding chooses how a map is written:

for encoding in ("mapping", "kv", "entries"):
    text = df.genson.normalise_json(
        "j", map_threshold=1, map_encoding=encoding, decode=False
    )
    print(f"{encoding:8s}", text[0])

mapping  {"id":1,"labels":{"en":"Hi","es":"Hola"}}
kv       {"id":1,"labels":[{"key":"en","value":"Hi"},{"key":"es","value":"Hola"}]}
entries  {"id":1,"labels":[{"en":"Hi"},{"es":"Hola"}]}
  • "mapping" (the default) writes a JSON object, which str.json_decode reads as a pl.Map.
  • "kv" writes a list of {"key": ..., "value": ...} objects, which it reads as a list of {key, value} structs (see below).
  • "entries" writes a list of one-key objects. No Polars dtype reads it, so it can't be decoded.

Pass the same map_encoding to infer_polars_schema or avro_to_polars_schema and the schema you get decodes the text:

text = df.genson.normalise_json("j", map_threshold=1, map_encoding="kv", decode=False)
dtype = pl.Struct(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", map_threshold=1, map_encoding="kv"))
print(text.str.json_decode(dtype).struct.unnest())

shape: (2, 2)
┌─────┬──────────────────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ labels                       │
│ --- ┆ ---                          │
│ i64 ┆ list[struct[2]]              │
╞═════╪══════════════════════════════╡
│ 1   ┆ [{"en","Hi"}, {"es","Hola"}] │
│ 2   ┆ [{"fr","Bonjour"}]           │
└─────┴──────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: In Parquet: a MAP
docs.text:
normalise_from_parquet(typed=True) writes the normalised rows as typed columns, and a map as a Parquet MAP. Polars reads it back as a pl.Map:

from polars_genson import normalise_from_parquet

df.write_parquet("labels.parquet")
normalise_from_parquet(
    "labels.parquet", column="j", output_path="typed.parquet", map_threshold=1, typed=True
)
print(pl.read_parquet_schema("typed.parquet")["j"])

Struct({'id': Int64, 'labels': Map(String, String)})

Other Parquet readers see a map too: pyarrow reads labels as map<string, string>.

The file's metadata holds the Avro schema and the options it was written with, including map_encoding, so its dtype can be rebuilt from the file alone:

from polars_genson import avro_to_polars_schema, read_parquet_metadata

meta = read_parquet_metadata("typed.parquet")
map_encoding = json.loads(meta["genson_normalise_config"])["map_encoding"]
print(avro_to_polars_schema(meta["genson_avro_schema"], map_encoding=map_encoding))

Schema({'id': Int64, 'labels': Map(String, String)})

docs.title: The kv encoding
docs.text:
A map can also be held as a list of {key, value} structs. Arrow and Parquet store a map this way underneath, and map.entries gives it from a pl.Map. A cast goes either way:

kv = pl.List(pl.Struct({"key": pl.String, "value": pl.String}))
print(out["labels"].cast(kv).to_list())

[[{'key': 'en', 'value': 'Hi'}, {'key': 'es', 'value': 'Hola'}], [{'key': 'fr', 'value': 'Bonjour'}]]

map_encoding="kv" gives this form everywhere: in the JSON text, the dtypes from infer_polars_schema, avro_to_polars_schema and normalise_json, and the typed Parquet columns. Use it when your code works with maps as lists, for example to explode a map into one row per key.

When you pass your own schema as normalise_json(decode=...), its maps decide the encoding: a pl.Map is decoded from JSON objects and a list of {key, value} structs from kv lists, unless you pass map_encoding yourself.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• schema_to_json writes a pl.Map as a list of {key, value} structs, the Arrow storage, because the Rust polars crate has no map dtype. json_to_schema reads it back as that list.
  • A map's keys are always strings, as in Avro.

docs.title: Maps and records: objects with fixed or varying keys
docs.text:
A JSON object can play two different roles:

  • A record has a fixed set of fields, like {"name": ..., "age": ...}. Each field is its own column, so it becomes a Polars struct.
  • A map has keys that are data, like {"en": "hello", "fr": "bonjour"} or scores keyed by subject. The keys vary from row to row, so making each key a struct field would give one field per distinct key. genson instead makes it a Polars map, pl.Map, where each row holds only its own keys.

genson decides which role an object plays from what it sees across all rows.

docs.title: How genson decides
docs.text:
An object becomes a map when it has more than map_threshold distinct keys across all rows (default 20) and its values all have the same type. Otherwise it stays a record.

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": [
    '{"scores": {"maths": 90, "art": 75}}',
    '{"scores": {"history": 60}}',
]})
print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j"))                   # 3 distinct keys: a record
print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", map_threshold=1))  # threshold lowered: a map

Schema({'scores': Struct({'maths': Int64, 'art': Int64, 'history': Int64})})
Schema({'scores': Map(String, Int64)})

As a record, scores has one field per subject seen in any row, and each row has nulls for the subjects it doesn't have. As a map, each row lists only its own subjects:

print(df.genson.normalise_json("j", map_threshold=1))

shape: (2, 1)
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ scores                   │
│ ---                      │
│ map[str, i64]            │
╞══════════════════════════╡
│ {"maths": 90, "art": 75} │
│ {"history": 60}          │
└──────────────────────────┘

Use a map when the keys are data (IDs, languages, dates, names) and a record when they are a known set of fields.

docs.title: Choosing per field
docs.text:
map_threshold applies to every object. To set the role of particular fields, use force_field_types:

print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", force_field_types={"scores": "record"}, map_threshold=1))

Schema({'scores': Struct({'maths': Int64, 'art': Int64, 'history': Int64})})

Forcing a field to "map" makes it a map whatever its number of keys, and its values keep their type:

print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", force_field_types={"scores": "map"}))

Schema({'scores': Map(String, Int64)})

If the values differ, genson unifies them the same way as for unify_maps below. Only values with no common type, such as numbers in some keys and strings in others, fall back to strings, so that no value is lost.

map_max_required_keys adds a second condition: an object with more than that many keys present in every row stays a record, however many keys it has in total.

docs.title: Maps of records that differ: unify_maps
docs.text:
When a map's values are themselves objects with different fields, they can't share one value type, so by default genson keeps the whole object as a record:

letters = pl.DataFrame({"j": [
    '{"letters": {"a": {"vowel": true, "n": 3}, "b": {"consonant": true, "n": 1}}}'
]})
print(letters.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", map_threshold=1))

Schema({'letters': Struct({'a': Struct({'vowel': Boolean, 'n': Int64}), 'b': Struct({'consonant': Boolean, 'n': Int64})})})

With unify_maps=True, genson merges the values into one record type, with a field for every field seen and nulls where a value lacks one, and the object becomes a map:

print(letters.genson.infer_polars_schema("j", map_threshold=1, unify_maps=True))
print(letters.genson.normalise_json("j", map_threshold=1, unify_maps=True)["letters"].to_list())

Schema({'letters': Map(String, Struct({'n': Int64, 'vowel': Boolean, 'consonant': Boolean}))})
[{'a': {'n': 3, 'vowel': True, 'consonant': None}, 'b': {'n': 1, 'vowel': None, 'consonant': True}}]

To keep particular fields out of this merging, list them in no_unify.

docs.title: How a map is stored
docs.text:
A map is a pl.Map in Polars and a MAP in typed Parquet output. In JSON text it's written as an object by default, and map_encoding="kv" gives lists of {key, value} structs instead, in the text and the dtypes alike. See Map types.

Empty maps become null by default, like empty arrays; see Nulls, missing keys and empty values.

docs.title: Mixed types in one field
docs.text: The same JSON field can hold different kinds of value in different rows. A Polars column has one dtype, so genson either finds a type that holds all of them or splits the field.

docs.title: A number, sometimes an integer and sometimes a float
docs.text:
Integers are widened to floats, and the column is Float64:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"x": 1}', '{"x": 1.5}']})
print(df.genson.normalise_json("j"))

shape: (2, 1)
┌─────┐
│ x   │
│ --- │
│ f64 │
╞═════╡
│ 1.0 │
│ 1.5 │
└─────┘

docs.title: A value, sometimes a scalar and sometimes an array
docs.text:
The scalar is wrapped into a one-item list, and the column is a list:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"x": "a"}', '{"x": ["b", "c"]}']})
print(df.genson.normalise_json("j"))

shape: (2, 1)
┌────────────┐
│ x          │
│ ---        │
│ list[str]  │
╞════════════╡
│ ["a"]      │
│ ["b", "c"] │
└────────────┘

docs.title: A value, sometimes a scalar and sometimes an object
docs.text:
The column becomes a struct, and the scalar is kept in an extra field named after the field and the scalar's type (x__string here). This is scalar promotion, controlled by wrap_scalars (on by default).

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"x": "plain"}', '{"x": {"amount": 3, "unit": "kg"}}']})
out = df.genson.normalise_json("j")
print(out.schema)
print(out["x"].to_list())

Schema({'x': Struct({'amount': Int64, 'unit': String, 'x__string': String})})
[{'amount': None, 'unit': None, 'x__string': 'plain'}, {'amount': 3, 'unit': 'kg', 'x__string': None}]

docs.title: Keeping a field's shape stable across files: force_scalar_promotion
docs.text:
If a field is a plain scalar in one file but an object in another, the two files get different schemas. force_scalar_promotion promotes the named fields even when every row is a scalar, so the field is always a struct:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"precision": 11}', '{"precision": 12}']})
out = df.genson.normalise_json("j", force_scalar_promotion={"precision"})
print(out.schema)
print(out["precision"].to_list())

Schema({'precision': Struct({'precision__integer': Int64})})
[{'precision__integer': 11}, {'precision__integer': 12}]

docs.title: Numbers and booleans written as strings: coerce_strings
docs.text:
With coerce_strings=True, a string in a numeric or boolean field is parsed into that type ("42" becomes 42). Strings that don't parse become null.

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"x": 1}', '{"x": "42"}']})
print(df.genson.normalise_json("j", coerce_strings=True))

shape: (2, 1)
┌─────┐
│ x   │
│ --- │
│ i64 │
╞═════╡
│ 1   │
│ 42  │
└─────┘

docs.title: Current limitation: different scalar types in one field
docs.text:
When a field holds different kinds of scalar, such as numbers in some rows and strings in others, genson keeps the first type in its precedence order (boolean, then integer, then number, then string), and values of the other types become null:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"j": ['{"x": 1}', '{"x": "a"}']})
print(df.genson.normalise_json("j"))

shape: (2, 1)
┌────────────┐
│ x          │
│ ---        │
│ struct[2]  │
╞════════════╡
│ {1,null}   │
│ {null,"a"} │
└────────────┘

If a field can hold numbers written as strings, coerce_strings=True recovers them. Otherwise, check such fields in the raw JSON before normalising.

docs.title: Nulls, missing keys and empty values
docs.text: JSON has several ways to say "nothing here": a key can be missing, a key can be null, an array or object can be empty, and a whole row can be null. A Polars column only has null, so genson has to decide which of these become null.

docs.title: What each one becomes
docs.text:
With default options, a missing key, a null value and an empty array all become null. An empty object in a field that holds records becomes a struct whose fields are null.

empty_as_null=True (the default)

Row a tags meta {"a": 1, "tags": ["x"], "meta": {"k": 1}} 1 ["x"] {"k": 1} key missing: {} null null null key is null: {"a": null, "tags": null, "meta": null} null null null empty values: {"tags": [], "meta": {}} null null {"k": null}

empty_as_null=False

Row a tags meta {"a": 1, "tags": ["x"], "meta": {"k": 1}} 1 ["x"] {"k": 1} key missing: {} null null null key is null: {"a": null, "tags": null, "meta": null} null null null empty values: {"tags": [], "meta": {}} null [] {"k": null}
  • A missing key and a null value give the same result. After normalising, you can't tell whether a field was absent or explicitly null. If that distinction matters, check the raw JSON before normalising.
  • Empty arrays become null by default. Pass empty_as_null=False to keep them as empty lists. The option also covers empty maps (objects whose keys vary, see Maps and records).
  • An empty object in a record field is not null. It becomes a struct with every field null ({"k": null} above), with or without empty_as_null, because a record's fields are fixed and each one is simply absent.
  • The dtype isn't affected. tags is List(String) either way. Only when a field is empty in every row does genson have no item type to infer, and then it uses List(Null) (see Type mapping).

docs.title: Null rows
docs.text:
A row that is null, rather than a JSON object, gives a row of nulls, so the output has exactly one row per input row and still lines up with the other columns:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2, 3], "j": ['{"a": 1}', None, '{"a": 3}']})
print(df.select("id").hstack(df.genson.normalise_json("j")))

shape: (3, 2)
┌─────┬──────┐
│ id  ┆ a    │
│ --- ┆ ---  │
│ i64 ┆ i64  │
╞═════╪══════╡
│ 1   ┆ 1    │
│ 2   ┆ null │
│ 3   ┆ 3    │
└─────┴──────┘

normalise_from_parquet does the same, and its keep_columns option copies other columns (such as an id) into the output file alongside the normalised one. See Normalise JSON stored in Parquet.

docs.title: How JSON types map to Polars dtypes
docs.text:
JSON has six kinds of value: strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and objects. A Polars column has exactly one dtype. When genson normalises a JSON column, it chooses one dtype per field that can hold every row's value, and converts each value to it.

The table below shows what normalise_json produces for two rows of each kind of input, with default options. It's generated from genson itself each time these docs are built.

Input JSON rows Polars dtype Values String {"x": "a"}{"x": "b"} String "a""b" Integer {"x": 1}{"x": 2} Int64 12 Float {"x": 1.5}{"x": 2.5} Float64 1.52.5 Integer and float {"x": 1}{"x": 1.5} Float64 1.01.5 Boolean {"x": true}{"x": false} Boolean truefalse Always null {"x": null}{"x": null} Null nullnull Sometimes null {"x": 1}{"x": null} Int64 1null Sometimes missing {"x": 1}{} Int64 1null Array {"x": ["a", "b"]}{"x": ["c"]} List(String) ["a", "b"]["c"] Empty array {"x": ["a"]}{"x": []} List(String) ["a"]null Always-empty array {"x": []}{"x": []} List(Null) nullnull String or array {"x": "a"}{"x": ["b", "c"]} List(String) ["a"]["b", "c"] Object (record) {"x": {"a": 1}}{"x": {"a": 2, "b": "z"}} Struct({'a': Int64, 'b': String}) {"a": 1, "b": null}{"a": 2, "b": "z"} Object with varying keys (map)(map_threshold=1) {"x": {"en": "hi"}}{"x": {"fr": "salut", "de": "hallo"}} Map(String, String) {"en": "hi"}{"fr": "salut", "de": "hallo"} Scalar or object {"x": "a"}{"x": {"n": 1}} Struct({'n': Int64, 'x__string': String}) {"n": null, "x__string": "a"}{"n": 1, "x__string": null}

docs.title: Reading the table
docs.text:
• Scalars map directly: strings to String, integers to Int64, floats to Float64, booleans to Boolean.
  • Integers and floats in the same field become Float64, with the integers widened (1 becomes 1.0).
  • Null and missing are the same after normalising. A key that is absent and a key whose value is null both give a null. See Nulls, missing keys and empty values.
  • Empty arrays become null by default, and an array that is empty in every row gets the dtype List(Null), since there is no item type to infer.
  • A value that is sometimes a string and sometimes an array becomes a list: the string is wrapped into a one-item list.
  • Objects become structs when their keys are a fixed set (a record), or pl.Map columns when their keys vary (a map). See Maps and records and Map types.
  • A value that is sometimes a scalar and sometimes an object becomes a struct, and the scalar is kept under a promoted field named after the field and its type (here x__string). See Mixed types.

docs.title: Guides
docs.text:
Each guide covers one task, with examples you can run. For why genson behaves as it does, see How it works.

  • Infer a schema from a JSON column: as a Polars schema, a JSON Schema or an Avro schema, per row or merged.
  • Normalise a JSON column: into typed columns, one struct column, or JSON strings.
  • Normalise JSON stored in Parquet: straight from a Parquet column to typed Parquet output, keeping other columns alongside.
  • Factor out repeated embedded data: store data that repeats per key once, in a lookup table.
  • Remove malformed records: leave out records holding named fields, and keep them in a separate file.
  • Process large inputs: speed and memory for big files.

docs.title: Factor out repeated embedded data
docs.text:
JSON documents often embed a full copy of the things they reference. An order carries its customer's details, and a Wikidata claim carries every language's label for the property and entity it points to. Such a field is invariant per key: every object with the same key carries the same value, so the key (its determinant) fixes it.

Every copy after the first is redundant, and genson would otherwise infer a schema for it, normalise it and write it out again for every row. extract_invariants on normalise_from_parquet removes these fields from the rows before inference and writes each distinct value once to a lookup table.

docs.title: Example: orders that embed their customer
docs.text:
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({"order": [
    '{"order": 1, "customer_id": 7, "customer": {"name": "Ada", "city": "London"}}',
    '{"order": 2, "customer_id": 8, "customer": {"name": "Bo", "city": "Oslo"}}',
    '{"order": 3, "customer_id": 7, "customer": {"name": "Ada", "city": "London"}}',
]}).write_parquet("orders.parquet")

customer is determined by customer_id, so extract it:

from polars_genson import normalise_from_parquet

normalise_from_parquet(
    "orders.parquet",
    column="order",
    output_path="slim.parquet",
    typed=True,
    extract_invariants={"customer": "customer_id"},
    lookup_output_path="customers.parquet",
)
print(pl.read_parquet("slim.parquet").unnest("order"))
print(pl.read_parquet("customers.parquet"))

shape: (3, 2)
┌───────┬─────────────┐
│ order ┆ customer_id │
│ ---   ┆ ---         │
│ i64   ┆ i64         │
╞═══════╪═════════════╡
│ 1     ┆ 7           │
│ 2     ┆ 8           │
│ 3     ┆ 7           │
└───────┴─────────────┘
shape: (2, 3)
┌──────────┬─────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ field    ┆ key ┆ value                          │
│ ---      ┆ --- ┆ ---                            │
│ str      ┆ str ┆ str                            │
╞══════════╪═════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ customer ┆ 7   ┆ {"name":"Ada","city":"London"} │
│ customer ┆ 8   ┆ {"name":"Bo","city":"Oslo"}    │
└──────────┴─────┴────────────────────────────────┘

The rows keep customer_id and lose customer. The lookup table has one row per distinct customer, with string columns field (which extracted field), key (the determinant's value) and value (the field as JSON), in the order first seen.

docs.title: Join the values back
docs.text:
The value column is JSON, so decode it with the dtype you want, then join on the key:

customers = pl.read_parquet("customers.parquet").select(
    pl.col("key").cast(pl.Int64).alias("customer_id"),
    pl.col("value").str.json_decode(pl.Struct({"name": pl.String, "city": pl.String})),
).unnest("value")
orders = pl.read_parquet("slim.parquet").unnest("order")
print(orders.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left"))

shape: (3, 4)
┌───────┬─────────────┬──────┬────────┐
│ order ┆ customer_id ┆ name ┆ city   │
│ ---   ┆ ---         ┆ ---  ┆ ---    │
│ i64   ┆ i64         ┆ str  ┆ str    │
╞═══════╪═════════════╪══════╪════════╡
│ 1     ┆ 7           ┆ Ada  ┆ London │
│ 2     ┆ 8           ┆ Bo   ┆ Oslo   │
│ 3     ┆ 7           ┆ Ada  ┆ London │
└───────┴─────────────┴──────┴────────┘

The lookup key is always a string, so cast it to the determinant's type before joining.

docs.title: Several fields at once
docs.text:
Pass one entry per field. Each field is found wherever it sits next to its determinant, at any depth, and the field column tells the lookup rows apart:

extract_invariants={"labels": "id", "property-labels": "property", "unit-labels": "unit"}

docs.title: A field that isn't invariant is an error
docs.text:
If one determinant value turns up with two different values of the field, extracting it would lose one of them, so genson raises an error instead:

pl.DataFrame({"order": [
    '{"customer_id": 7, "customer": {"name": "Ada"}}',
    '{"customer_id": 7, "customer": {"name": "Ada Lovelace"}}',
]}).write_parquet("conflict.parquet")

try:
    normalise_from_parquet(
        "conflict.parquet", column="order", output_path="out.parquet", typed=True,
        extract_invariants={"customer": "customer_id"}, lookup_output_path="lookup.parquet",
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)

extract_invariants: field 'customer' is not invariant for its determinant 'customer_id' ('7' has two different values)

docs.title: When it's worth it
docs.text: The more often each key repeats, and the larger its value, the more work extraction saves. On a 615 MB chunk of Wikidata claims, where each entity's multilingual label maps are embedded in every claim that mentions it, extraction took normalisation from 22 s to 4.2 s and peak memory from 9.6 GB to 4.2 GB.

docs.title: Infer a schema from a JSON column
docs.text: genson reads every row of a JSON string column and infers one schema that fits them all. You can get that schema as a Polars schema, as a JSON Schema, or as an Avro schema.

docs.title: As a Polars schema
docs.text:
infer_polars_schema gives the dtypes that normalise_json will produce:

import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"json": [
    '{"id": 1, "name": "Ada", "tags": ["x"]}',
    '{"id": 2, "name": "Bo", "email": "bo@example.com"}',
]})
print(df.genson.infer_polars_schema("json"))

Schema({'id': Int64, 'name': String, 'tags': List(String), 'email': String})

docs.title: As a JSON Schema
docs.text:
infer_json_schema returns the schema as a dict. required lists the fields present in every row:

import json

print(json.dumps(df.genson.infer_json_schema("json"), indent=2))

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/schema#",
  "properties": {
    "id": {
      "type": "integer"
    },
    "name": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "tags": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "string"
      }
    },
    "email": {
      "type": "string"
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "id",
    "name"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}

Pass avro=True for an Avro schema instead:

print(json.dumps(df.genson.infer_json_schema("json", avro=True), indent=2))

{
  "type": "record",
  "name": "document",
  "namespace": "genson",
  "fields": [
    {
      "name": "id",
      "type": "int"
    },
    {
      "name": "name",
      "type": "string"
    },
    {
      "name": "tags",
      "type": [
        "null",
        {
          "type": "array",
          "items": "string"
        }
      ]
    },
    {
      "name": "email",
      "type": [
        "null",
        "string"
      ]
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: One schema per row
docs.text:
With merge_schemas=False, infer_json_schema returns each row's own schema instead of one merged schema, which helps when you want to see which rows differ:

for schema in df.genson.infer_json_schema("json", merge_schemas=False):
    print(sorted(schema["properties"]))

['id', 'name', 'tags']
['email', 'id', 'name']

docs.title: When each row is itself a map: wrap_root
docs.text:
Sometimes the top level of each row has keys that are data, such as one key per language. genson never makes the top level of a row a map (no_root_map=True), so each key would become its own field:

labels = pl.DataFrame({"json": ['{"en": "hello"}', '{"fr": "bonjour", "de": "hallo"}']})
print(labels.genson.infer_polars_schema("json", map_threshold=1))

Schema({'en': String, 'fr': String, 'de': String})

wrap_root wraps every row under a key first, so the row becomes a field that can be a map:

print(labels.genson.infer_polars_schema("json", map_threshold=1, wrap_root="labels"))

Schema({'labels': Map(String, String)})

docs.title: Rows in other framings
docs.text:
• Newline-delimited JSON in one string: pass ndjson=True.
  • A top-level array of objects is read as one object per element (ignore_outer_array=True, the default).

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Type mapping for how each kind of JSON value is typed.
  • Maps and records for map_threshold, force_field_types and unify_maps.
  • Normalise a JSON column to get the data in the inferred shape.

docs.title: Process large inputs
docs.text: For large JSON data, three things make the biggest difference to speed and memory: the route the data takes, how much redundant data it carries, and how many row schemas are held at once during inference.

docs.title: Use normalise_from_parquet with typed=True
docs.text: The DataFrame methods (df.genson.normalise_json and friends) work on data already loaded into Polars. For data in a Parquet file, normalise_from_parquet does the whole job in Rust: it reads the column, infers, normalises and writes the result, without a DataFrame in between. With typed=True it writes typed columns directly, instead of writing JSON strings that then have to be parsed again. See Normalise JSON stored in Parquet.

docs.title: Remove repeated embedded data
docs.text: If the JSON carries the same nested value in many rows (a customer embedded in every order, a label map in every reference to an entity), extract it with extract_invariants. The work then scales with the number of distinct values rather than the number of copies. See Factor out repeated embedded data.

docs.title: Limit memory during inference: max_builders
docs.text:
Schema inference builds a schema for every row in parallel (on a thread pool the size of your CPU core count), then merges them into one. By default every row's schema is held in memory until that single merge, so peak memory grows with the number of rows.

max_builders caps this: rows are processed in chunks of max_builders, and each chunk's schemas are merged before the next chunk starts. With 1,000,000 rows and max_builders=1000, at most 1000 row schemas are held at once.

schema = df.genson.infer_polars_schema("json", max_builders=1000)

max_builders is accepted by infer_json_schema, infer_polars_schema, normalise_json, infer_from_parquet and normalise_from_parquet. Smaller values lower peak memory at some cost in speed.

docs.title: See where the time goes: profile=True
docs.text: Pass profile=True to print how long each step takes (reading, inference, normalisation, writing) to standard error. It's the quickest way to tell which of the steps above will help.

docs.title: Normalise a JSON column into typed columns
docs.text: normalise_json infers a schema for a JSON string column, rewrites every row to fit it, and decodes the result into typed Polars columns.

docs.title: Typed columns (the default)
docs.text:
import polars as pl
import polars_genson

df = pl.DataFrame({"json": [
    '{"id": 1, "name": "Ada", "tags": ["x"]}',
    '{"id": 2, "name": "Bo", "email": "bo@example.com"}',
]})
print(df.genson.normalise_json("json"))

shape: (2, 4)
┌─────┬──────┬───────────┬────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ name ┆ tags      ┆ email          │
│ --- ┆ ---  ┆ ---       ┆ ---            │
│ i64 ┆ str  ┆ list[str] ┆ str            │
╞═════╪══════╪═══════════╪════════════════╡
│ 1   ┆ Ada  ┆ ["x"]     ┆ null           │
│ 2   ┆ Bo   ┆ null      ┆ bo@example.com │
└─────┴──────┴───────────┴────────────────┘

Each field becomes a column, and rows that lack a field get null.

docs.title: One struct column: unnest=False
docs.text:
To keep the result as a single struct column, pass unnest=False. The result is a one-column DataFrame, so it can sit alongside the original columns:

print(df.hstack(df.genson.normalise_json("json", unnest=False).rename({"json": "parsed"})))

shape: (2, 2)
┌─────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ json                            ┆ parsed                         │
│ ---                             ┆ ---                            │
│ str                             ┆ struct[4]                      │
╞═════════════════════════════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ {"id": 1, "name": "Ada", "tags… ┆ {1,"Ada",["x"],null}           │
│ {"id": 2, "name": "Bo", "email… ┆ {2,"Bo",null,"bo@example.com"} │
└─────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: JSON strings: decode=False
docs.text:
decode=False returns the normalised rows as JSON strings. Every row then has every field:

print(df.genson.normalise_json("json", decode=False).to_list())

['{"id":1,"name":"Ada","tags":["x"],"email":null}', '{"id":2,"name":"Bo","tags":null,"email":"bo@example.com"}']

docs.title: A schema you already have: decode=schema
docs.text:
If you already know the schema, for example from infer_polars_schema on an earlier batch, pass it as decode. genson decodes with it directly and skips inferring the schema for decoding:

schema = df.genson.infer_polars_schema("json")
print(df.genson.normalise_json("json", decode=schema))

shape: (2, 4)
┌─────┬──────┬───────────┬────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ name ┆ tags      ┆ email          │
│ --- ┆ ---  ┆ ---       ┆ ---            │
│ i64 ┆ str  ┆ list[str] ┆ str            │
╞═════╪══════╪═══════════╪════════════════╡
│ 1   ┆ Ada  ┆ ["x"]     ┆ null           │
│ 2   ┆ Bo   ┆ null      ┆ bo@example.com │
└─────┴──────┴───────────┴────────────────┘

docs.title: Options that change the output
docs.text:
• empty_as_null (default True): empty arrays and maps become null. See Nulls and empty values.
  • coerce_strings: parse numbers and booleans written as strings. See Mixed types.
  • map_threshold, force_field_types, unify_maps: how objects become maps or records. See Maps and records.
  • map_encoding: how maps are written as JSON, and the dtype they decode to. See Map types.
  • wrap_scalars and force_scalar_promotion: how scalars that collide with objects are kept. See Mixed types.

For data in Parquet files, normalise_from_parquet does the same without loading the data into a DataFrame.

docs.title: Normalise JSON stored in Parquet
docs.text:
When your JSON is a string column in a Parquet file, normalise_from_parquet reads it, infers a schema, normalises every row and writes a new Parquet file, all in Rust, without loading the data into a Polars DataFrame first. This is the fastest route for large files and uses the least memory.

The examples on this page use this file:

import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["Q1", "Q2", "Q3"],
    "data": [
        '{"name": "Alice", "tags": ["a", "b"], "labels": {"en": "Alice", "fr": "Alice"}}',
        '{"name": "Bob", "tags": [], "labels": {"de": "Bob"}}',
        None,
    ],
}).write_parquet("input.parquet")

docs.title: Write typed columns: typed=True
docs.text:
With typed=True, the output column is a Polars struct you can read directly. Use keep_columns to carry other input columns, such as an id, into the output:

from polars_genson import normalise_from_parquet

normalise_from_parquet(
    "input.parquet",
    column="data",
    output_path="typed.parquet",
    map_threshold=2,
    typed=True,
    keep_columns=["id"],
)
print(pl.read_parquet("typed.parquet").unnest("data"))

shape: (3, 4)
┌─────┬───────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ name  ┆ tags       ┆ labels                         │
│ --- ┆ ---   ┆ ---        ┆ ---                            │
│ str ┆ str   ┆ list[str]  ┆ map[str, str]                  │
╞═════╪═══════╪════════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ Q1  ┆ Alice ┆ ["a", "b"] ┆ {"en": "Alice", "fr": "Alice"} │
│ Q2  ┆ Bob   ┆ null       ┆ {"de": "Bob"}                  │
│ Q3  ┆ null  ┆ null       ┆ null                           │
└─────┴───────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
  • labels has varying keys, so with map_threshold=2 it becomes a map, stored as a Parquet MAP and read back as a pl.Map (see Map types).
  • The empty tags list is null (see Nulls and empty values).
  • The null input row stays a null row, so the output has one row per input row and the kept id column lines up with it.

typed=True takes map_encoding="mapping" (the default) or "kv", which stores maps as lists of {key, value} structs.

With unnest=True, the struct's fields are written as top-level columns after the keep_columns, as DataFrame.unnest makes them (a null row is null in each column), so the file reads back without the .unnest("data"). A kept column with the same name as one of the struct's fields is an error.

docs.title: Write files in a shared schema: schema=
docs.text:
Files normalised one at a time but read together, such as chunks of a large dataset or shards processed in parallel, need one schema between them. Each file's inferred schema is only what its own rows hold: a nested field no row of a chunk has is missing from that chunk's file, and a field null in every row has the dtype Null. Pass the dataset's schema as schema, and every file is written in it, however little of it a file's rows use.

genson still infers each file's schema, and uses it twice:

  • it checks it against yours before writing, so a file holding data your schema has no place for (a new field, a string where you have an integer) stops with an error naming the field, rather than losing the data or writing another schema;
  • it keeps it in the file's metadata, so you can see what each file actually held.

The rows are put into your schema's shape as they are written, in the same pass.

Take two chunks of one dataset. No row of chunk_a has a postcode or a score:

pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["a1", "a2"],
    "data": [
        '{"name": "Alice", "address": {"city": "Paris"}, "score": null}',
        '{"name": "Ana", "address": {"city": "Lisbon"}, "score": null}',
    ],
}).write_parquet("chunk_a.parquet")

pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["b1", "b2"],
    "data": [
        '{"name": "Bob", "address": {"city": "Rome", "postcode": "00100"}, "score": 3}',
        '{"name": "Bea", "address": null, "score": 7}',
    ],
}).write_parquet("chunk_b.parquet")

schema is the output column's fields, as a pl.Schema (or a pl.Struct), and needs typed=True:

stored = pl.Schema({
    "name": pl.String,
    "address": pl.Struct({"city": pl.String, "postcode": pl.String}),
    "score": pl.Int64,
})

for chunk in ["a", "b"]:
    normalise_from_parquet(
        f"chunk_{chunk}.parquet",
        column="data",
        output_path=f"out_{chunk}.parquet",
        typed=True,
        keep_columns=["id"],
        schema=stored,
        unnest=True,
    )

print(pl.read_parquet("out_*.parquet"))

shape: (4, 4)
┌─────┬───────┬──────────────────┬───────┐
│ id  ┆ name  ┆ address          ┆ score │
│ --- ┆ ---   ┆ ---              ┆ ---   │
│ str ┆ str   ┆ struct[2]        ┆ i64   │
╞═════╪═══════╪══════════════════╪═══════╡
│ a1  ┆ Alice ┆ {"Paris",null}   ┆ null  │
│ a2  ┆ Ana   ┆ {"Lisbon",null}  ┆ null  │
│ b1  ┆ Bob   ┆ {"Rome","00100"} ┆ 3     │
│ b2  ┆ Bea   ┆ null             ┆ 7     │
└─────┴───────┴──────────────────┴───────┘

Both files have the schema's columns and dtypes, its fields in its order at every depth: chunk_a's address.postcode is null in each row, and its score, Null in its inferred schema, is written as the schema's Int64. A null value stays null (Bea's address).

docs.title: Which inferred schemas fit: schema_check
docs.text:
The inferred schema is checked against schema before anything is written. With schema_check="compatible" (the default) it fits when, recursively:

inferred fits the schema's Null (no value seen) any dtype a dtype same dtype (no widening: Int64 does not fit Float64) a struct struct holding each of its fields, each fitting (the schema may have more) a list, an array, a map list, array of the same size, or map whose items (keys and values) fit

A schema field typed Null takes only Null: a value there is data the schema has no type for. Anything else raises ValueError, one line per offending field, its path written with . between fields, [] for a list's items and {} for a map's values:

pl.DataFrame({
    "id": ["c1"],
    "data": ['{"name": "Cy", "address": {"city": "Oslo", "floor": 3}, "score": "high"}'],
}).write_parquet("chunk_c.parquet")

try:
    normalise_from_parquet(
        "chunk_c.parquet",
        column="data",
        output_path="out_c.parquet",
        typed=True,
        schema=stored,
    )
except ValueError as e:
    print(e)
print(os.path.exists("out_c.parquet"))

The inferred schema of 'data' does not fit the target schema (schema_check="compatible"):
  address.floor: a field the target schema lacks (Int64)
  score: String, the target has Int64
False

Nothing is written for a file that fails, including its lookup and pruned files.

With schema_check="strict" the inferred schema must be the schema, field for field, so a missing field, or a Null where the schema has another dtype, is an error too: chunk_a fails it. Use it when every file is expected to use the whole schema. With schema_check="none" nothing is checked: fields the schema lacks are dropped, and other scalar dtypes are cast (an error if a value can't be).

docs.title: Check a schema without writing: check_schema_compatibility
docs.text:
A file written in a schema keeps the schema inferred from its rows in its genson_avro_schema metadata. check_schema_compatibility(inferred, target) gives the same verdict as schema_check for any two schemas, as a list of problems, empty when the inferred schema fits:

from polars_genson import (
    avro_to_polars_schema,
    check_schema_compatibility,
    read_parquet_metadata,
)

meta = read_parquet_metadata("out_a.parquet")
inferred_a = pl.Schema(avro_to_polars_schema(meta["genson_avro_schema"]))
print(inferred_a)
print(check_schema_compatibility(inferred_a, stored))
print(check_schema_compatibility(inferred_a, stored, schema_check="strict"))

Schema({'name': String, 'address': Struct({'city': String}), 'score': Null})
[]
['address.postcode: missing, and the schema check is strict', 'score: Null, the target has Int64']

docs.title: What the file holds
docs.text:
The columns have the schema's dtypes, laid out as Polars writes them to Parquet (strings and lists with 64-bit offsets, list items named element), so readers that take the Arrow schema from the file, such as pyarrow, see one schema across files.

schema takes strings, binaries, booleans, nulls, integers, floats, structs, lists, arrays and maps; other dtypes (dates and times, decimals, categoricals, enums) raise ValueError.

docs.title: Write JSON strings instead
docs.text:
Without typed=True, the output column holds each normalised row as a JSON string. The inferred schema is stored in the file's metadata, so you can decode the strings later:

from polars_genson import avro_to_polars_schema, read_parquet_metadata

normalise_from_parquet(
    "input.parquet", column="data", output_path="strings.parquet", map_threshold=2
)
meta = read_parquet_metadata("strings.parquet")
dtype = pl.Struct(avro_to_polars_schema(meta["genson_avro_schema"]))
decoded = pl.read_parquet("strings.parquet").select(pl.col("data").str.json_decode(dtype))
print(decoded.unnest("data"))

shape: (3, 3)
┌───────┬────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
│ name  ┆ tags       ┆ labels                         │
│ ---   ┆ ---        ┆ ---                            │
│ str   ┆ list[str]  ┆ map[str, str]                  │
╞═══════╪════════════╪════════════════════════════════╡
│ Alice ┆ ["a", "b"] ┆ {"en": "Alice", "fr": "Alice"} │
│ Bob   ┆ null       ┆ {"de": "Bob"}                  │
│ null  ┆ null       ┆ null                           │
└───────┴────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

If the strings were written with map_encoding="kv", pass the same to avro_to_polars_schema; the file's genson_normalise_config metadata records it.

This gives the same values as the typed output. Typed output skips writing every row as JSON and parsing it again, so it's faster and needs less memory; use strings when you need the JSON itself.

Both output forms store two metadata entries, which read_parquet_metadata returns: genson_avro_schema (the inferred schema as Avro JSON) and genson_normalise_config (the options used).

docs.title: Only infer the schema
docs.text:
infer_from_parquet returns the inferred schema without writing any data. It takes the same inference options as df.genson.infer_json_schema:

import json
from polars_genson import infer_from_parquet

schema = infer_from_parquet("input.parquet", column="data", map_threshold=2)
print(json.dumps(schema, indent=2))

{
  "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/schema#",
  "properties": {
    "name": {
      "type": "string"
    },
    "tags": {
      "type": "array",
      "items": {
        "type": "string"
      }
    },
    "labels": {
      "type": "object",
      "additionalProperties": {
        "type": "string"
      }
    }
  },
  "required": [
    "labels",
    "name",
    "tags"
  ],
  "type": "object"
}

Pass output_path to write the schema to a file instead, and avro=True for an Avro schema.

docs.title: Write Arrow data with genson's writer: write_parquet
docs.text:
write_parquet writes any Arrow data with the Parquet writer genson writes its own output with. It takes anything with an __arrow_c_stream__ method (a pyarrow.Table or RecordBatchReader, a Polars DataFrame, or the stream normalise_from_parquet(..., output_format="arrow") returns), without copying its buffers:

import pyarrow as pa
from polars_genson import write_parquet

table = pa.table({
    "id": ["Q1", "Q2"],
    "refs": [[{"hash": "a", "snaks": ["P1", "P2"]}], None],
})
write_parquet(table, "arrow.parquet", row_group_size=1_000_000)
print(pl.read_parquet("arrow.parquet"))

shape: (2, 2)
┌─────┬──────────────────────┐
│ id  ┆ refs                 │
│ --- ┆ ---                  │
│ str ┆ list[struct[2]]      │
╞═════╪══════════════════════╡
│ Q1  ┆ [{"a",["P1", "P2"]}] │
│ Q2  ┆ null                 │
└─────┴──────────────────────┘

Each row group's leaf columns are encoded in parallel, with the GIL released, so deeply nested tables, whose leaves a writer otherwise encodes one at a time, write several times faster: Wikidata's claims, one row per statement with their references and qualifiers (1.56 million rows), in 2.3 s on 4 threads against pyarrow's 8.5 s, 5% smaller.

The file holds the same data in the same Arrow schema as pyarrow.parquet writes it: list and map groups take the specification's names (element, key_value), and the Arrow schema is stored in the file's metadata. It is compressed with zstd (level 1), and each leaf column is dictionary encoded but one whose first values are mostly distinct.

The writer is pq-glue's (pq_glue::write), which genson's writer moved to: genson calls it from Rust, and writes the same files it wrote before. For its other engines and options (sorting columns, content-defined chunking, a bound on the threads), use pq_glue.write_parquet.

docs.title: See also
docs.text:
• Factor out repeated embedded data, for JSON that carries the same nested data in many rows.
  • Remove malformed records, for JSON with broken records to leave out.
  • Process large inputs, for memory use on big files.

docs.title: Remove malformed records
docs.text:
Real JSON sometimes holds records that are broken in a recognisable way: an entry that carries an error field instead of its data, or a bare string where every other row has an object. genson normalises these like any other record, so they reach the output, and the fields only they have (error, a promoted …__string) widen the schema for every row.

prune on normalise_from_parquet names those fields. Every record holding one is removed during normalisation and written to a separate file, and the fields are left out of the output schema.

docs.title: Example: sensor readings with failures
docs.text:
import polars as pl

pl.DataFrame({
    "sensor": ["a", "b", "c"],
    "data": [
        '{"readings": [{"t": 1, "value": 3.2, "calibration": {"offset": 0.1}}, {"t": 2, "error": "timeout"}]}',
        '{"readings": [{"t": 1, "value": 2.8, "calibration": "pending"}]}',
        '{"readings": [{"t": 1, "value": 1.5}]}',
    ],
}).write_parquet("sensors.parquet")

Sensor a has a failed reading holding error. Sensor b's calibration is the string "pending" where the others have an object, so genson promotes it to the field calibration__string. Prune both:

from polars_genson import normalise_from_parquet

normalise_from_parquet(
    "sensors.parquet",
    column="data",
    output_path="clean.parquet",
    typed=True,
    keep_columns=["sensor"],
    prune={"error", "calibration__string"},
    prune_output_path="pruned.parquet",
)
print(pl.read_parquet("clean.parquet").unnest("data"))
print(pl.read_parquet("pruned.parquet"))

shape: (3, 2)
┌────────┬─────────────────┐
│ sensor ┆ readings        │
│ ---    ┆ ---             │
│ str    ┆ list[struct[3]] │
╞════════╪═════════════════╡
│ a      ┆ [{1,3.2,{0.1}}] │
│ b      ┆ null            │
│ c      ┆ [{1,1.5,null}]  │
└────────┴─────────────────┘
shape: (2, 3)
┌────────┬────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
│ sensor ┆ path           ┆ value                           │
│ ---    ┆ ---            ┆ ---                             │
│ str    ┆ str            ┆ str                             │
╞════════╪════════════════╪═════════════════════════════════╡
│ a      ┆ ["readings",1] ┆ {"t":2,"error":"timeout"}       │
│ b      ┆ ["readings",0] ┆ {"t":1,"value":2.8,"calibratio… │
└────────┴────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

docs.title: What gets removed
docs.text:
• A record is pruned if it holds a non-null value for a named field, at any depth.
  • Names are the fields of the inferred schema, so a scalar promoted to a record goes by its promoted name, as it appears in the schema (calibration__string).
  • A pruned record that is a field of another record takes that record with it, since the record is incomplete without it. This goes on up to an array element or map entry, which is removed on its own. Above, the pending calibration takes its reading with it.
  • An array or map left empty by pruning is removed from its array or map, or is null as a record field. Sensor b's readings are null for this reason, while the row itself is kept. An array or map already empty in the input is normalised as usual.
  • The named fields are left out of the output schema.

docs.title: The pruned values
docs.text:
Nothing is dropped silently. prune_output_path gets one row per pruned value:

  • the keep_columns of its row, to tell which row it came from;
  • path: the keys and array indices from the row's root to the value, as a JSON array;
  • value: the value as it was in the input, as JSON.

prune and prune_output_path must be given together.

docs.title: Finding the names
docs.text: Infer the schema first and look for fields that only the malformed records have: an error or message, or a …__string beside a record's usual fields. See Mixed types for how promoted names are formed.

docs.title: The performance scorecard
docs.text:
scripts/scorecard.py measures where genson-core spends its instructions, time and memory, stage by stage, and how one revision changes that against another. On a pull request labelled perf-scorecard a workflow runs it against the PR's base and posts the report as one comment, updated on each push.

It measures the engine (genson-core), not a downstream pipeline: fixed workloads, generated from fixed seeds, that stand for the shapes of JSON genson meets.

docs.title: What it measures
docs.text:
For each revision and each corpus:

how why instructions, by stage callgrind, one thread, the release build repeatable to the instruction, so a change of 1% is real instructions per byte the above over the corpus's size comparable across corpora and as they grow wall and CPU time the release build, all threads, interleaved ABBA what users wait for allocations, bytes, peak live heap, by stage a debug build with alloc-stats, one thread what the allocator does (the counts do not depend on optimisation) peak RSS the timing runs memory as the system sees it (the input included) the output a hash of the schema (or of the normalised rows), and the processed count a speed-up that changes the output is not a speed-up

Each corpus is reported on its own. There is no aggregate score: a gain on one corpus that costs another shows as such.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
Each stage runs in a function of its own in genson-core/src/phase.rs, never inlined, so callgrind attributes the stage's instructions by name whatever is inlined within it. The stages run in turn and none holds another, so their costs add up; what none holds (the config's clone, freeing the input's results, rayon's own work) is reported as unattributed, and the total is the run's.

stage what runs in it rows reading the rows: their interned states (RowStates::row), or on the usual paths each row's builder merged into its chunk's and the chunks' into one merge the interned states merged into the builder (add_interned_row_chunks) write_schema the builder's schema written out: as a DAG (to_dag), or as Values when debugging rewrite fields forced to be maps, then map inference and unification (rewrite_objects) materialise the rewritten DAG as a Value reorder union types put in order (reorder_unions) avro the conversion to Avro (avrotize) normalise normalising rows to a schema (normalise_values), in the normalise workload

A stage is one call, so the markers cost nothing measurable when the scorecard is not running; the allocation counting exists only with the alloc-stats feature.

A revision from before the markers is attributed by the functions the stages run, the largest inclusive cost of each (LEGACY in the script). Inlining can hide some of them, so the report says when it has done this, and its stages are approximate.

docs.title: Corpora
docs.text:
Generated by genson-core/examples/scorecard.rs from fixed seeds, so no data is committed and every revision sees the same bytes. The workload uses only infer_json_schema_from_strings and its config (and normalise_values), so that revisions from before the scorecard can be measured with it: the script copies the checkout's workload into each revision's worktree.

corpus rows what it exercises claims 2,000 Wikidata-like claims objects, 15 MB (each property's values of one datatype, as in Wikidata) wikidata-pq's config: the interned path, map inference and unification of many properties, forced records and promoted scalars, Avro events 20,000 event logs of several kinds records that differ by kind, the defaults narrow 100,000 small records the row phase on many short rows labels 1,000 maps of languages' labels a map of records entities 150 wide Wikidata-like entities wide, varied records (Avro off: converting their schema is avrotize's cost) usual the event logs, payload forced to be a map a field forced to be a map: once the usual path (per-row builders), now the interned path forcing each distinct row (the name kept, to compare with earlier scorecards) normalise the claims, normalised to their inferred schema normalisation (inference is done before the runs)

docs.title: Times
docs.text:
Short runs on a shared machine are noisy, and the second of two runs back to back tends to be faster. So each process times a warm-up run and a measured one, the revisions take turns in the order base, head, head, base and so on, and the report gives the median with a verdict: faster or slower only when the change is at least 3% and the two revisions' interquartile ranges do not overlap, and the instructions moved too (by more than 0.5%), otherwise inconclusive: a time that moves with no change in instructions is noise.

Stage changes are listed only when both revisions have the stage markers. A revision attributed by function name puts what inlining hides under unattributed, so its stages are shown but not compared; the totals are exact either way.

docs.title: Running it
docs.text:
# Two revisions: builds each in .scorecard/, measures both, writes scorecard-out/report.md
python3 scripts/scorecard.py compare --base perf/dag-build --head perf/sibling-groups

# And the head against a third revision too (say, the stack's root)
python3 scripts/scorecard.py compare --base HEAD~1 --head HEAD --cumulative master

# A report from two measurements already made
python3 scripts/scorecard.py report scorecard-out/scorecard-<base>.json scorecard-out/scorecard-<head>.json

It needs git, cargo, valgrind (with callgrind_annotate) and Python 3, and takes about half an hour for two revisions: two release builds and two debug builds, seven callgrind runs each, and the timing rounds (--rounds, default 6).

docs.title: On pull requests
docs.text:
.github/workflows/scorecard.yml runs when a PR is labelled perf-scorecard, and then again on each push to it, on reopening, and when its base is changed; or by hand (workflow_dispatch, with any two revisions). It is not a required check.

  • One comment. The bot keeps one comment per PR, found by its hidden marker (<!-- genson-core-scorecard -->), and edits it on each run. It names the base and head compared, when, and the run.
  • Never stale. A newer run cancels an older one. Before editing, the comment job reads the PR's head and base again: if the head has moved, it leaves the comment to the newer run; if the base has moved (a stacked PR's base branch was pushed to), it publishes with a note that the base has moved, and the next push or a new label measures against it. A failed run replaces the results with a notice and the run's link, the previous results kept below it marked stale.
  • The base is the PR's base commit. A PR stacked on another is compared with the PR below it, so each change is credited to the PR that made it. The label perf-scorecard-cumulative adds a comparison of the head with master.
  • Two jobs. measure runs the PR's code with a read-only token and uploads the JSON and the report as an artifact (kept 90 days), and writes the report to the job summary. comment runs none of the PR's code: it downloads the report and posts or updates the bot's one comment.
  • Forks. A fork's PR gets a read-only token, so it gets the artifact and the summary but no comment. Commenting on those needs a workflow_run workflow on the default branch, which reads the artifact of a finished run; it can be added once this is on master.

docs.title: The JSON
docs.text:
scorecard-<sha>.json, one per revision:

{"rev": "perf/sibling-groups", "sha": "4eae9d0...",
 "corpora": {"claims": {
   "rows": 2000, "bytes": 15078434, "processed": 1985, "schema_hash": "…", "attribution": "markers",
   "instructions": {"total": 812000000, "stages": {"rows": 520000000, "merge": …}, "unattributed": …},
   "timing": {"wall": […], "cpu": […], "peak_rss_kb": […]},
   "allocations": [{"stage": "rows", "allocations": …, "bytes": …, "peak_live": …}, …]}}}

The artifacts are the history: plotting a series of them shows the engine's costs over time, stage by stage.

docs.title: Not yet covered
docs.text:
• Parquet reading and writing, and normalising straight into Arrow (both behind the parquet feature), and extract: workloads and stages for them are the next to add.
  • Wall time by stage: the stages' times could be recorded as their allocations are.
  • A history kept between runs (say, on a branch of its own) rather than in artifacts.

docs.title: Changing it
docs.text:
• A stage: add it to stages! in phase.rs, wrap the code it covers, and add it to STAGES (and, if older revisions run it, LEGACY) in the script. Stages must not hold one another.
  • A corpus: add it to corpus and CORPORA in the workload. Keep it to a fraction of a second (callgrind runs it some fifty times slower), and never change an existing one's seed or size without saying so, as that resets its history.

docs.title: Performance and diagnostics
